title: Test Your Understanding: Design a URL Shortener
description: Read-heavy design, caching redirects, and ID encoding — trade-offs from the case study.

questions.question: Why is a URL shortener considered read-heavy?

options.text: Creates (shorten) vastly outnumber redirects
Redirects dominate traffic — often 100:1 or more reads vs writes
Storage size is the main bottleneck
Short codes require full table scans

questions.explanation: Every click is a redirect (read). New links are created far less often. Architecture should optimize the redirect path with cache and indexed lookups.

questions.question: Base62 encoding of an auto-increment ID is attractive because:

options.text: It eliminates the need for a database
It produces compact codes without collision retries
It makes codes cryptographically secure
It requires no unique index

questions.explanation: Monotonic IDs encode to unique fixed-length strings. Random codes need uniqueness checks/retries. Predictability can be a downside for obscure links.

questions.question: For redirect caching, cache-aside means:

options.text: The database pushes every write to Redis synchronously
The app reads cache first, loads DB on miss, then populates cache
The CDN replaces Redis entirely
Redirects never use cache

questions.explanation: Cache-aside on GET /{code}: Redis holds short_code → long_url. Miss hits Postgres with unique index on short_code, then sets Redis with TTL.

questions.question: HTTP 301 vs 302 for redirects matters because:

options.text: 301 is temporary; browsers always revalidate
301 permanent redirects may be cached aggressively by clients — hard to change destination later
302 cannot include a Location header
Only 301 works with HTTPS

questions.explanation: 302/307 leave room to update or disable links. 301 is for permanent moves — fine if destinations never change.

questions.question: Click analytics on every redirect should ideally:

options.text: UPDATE the urls row synchronously before returning 302
Block redirect until analytics DB commits
Emit an async event after responding — decouple from hot path
Store counts only in Redis with no durability

questions.explanation: Redirect latency is user-facing. Async events to a queue/warehouse avoid hot-row writes on viral links.

questions.question: Caching '__NULL__' for unknown short codes helps with:

options.text: Cache stampede on hot keys
Cache penetration — repeated requests for non-existent codes
Write-through consistency
Sharding by short_code

questions.explanation: Negative caching (short TTL) stops junk codes from hammering DB on every request.

questions.question: A unique index on short_code is essential for redirect performance at scale.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Redirect is a point lookup by code. Without a unique index, each redirect devolves into a scan — unacceptable at thousands of QPS.

questions.question: Which are sensible v1 scope boundaries for a URL shortener interview design? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Defer full analytics dashboard to v2
Require multi-region active-active writes on day one
Focus on redirect latency and cache-aside
Blocklist malicious URLs on create

questions.explanation: Scope control: nail redirect path, caching, ID generation. Analytics, vanity aliases, and global active-active are often v2 unless requirements demand them.
